catalog_quote: [Verstraete 2021, ms. pp. 26-28] As already mentioned, there are three Lamalamic languages, viz. Umbuygamu, Lamalama and Rimanggudinhma. All three show full initial consonant loss, and all three largely conform to the typical onset-sensitive system predicted by the classic stress shift model, i.e. stress on the first consonant-initial syllable in the root, as illustrated in (22). ... Rimanggudinhma (Verstraete 2017) e. arho ‘arm’ /aˈr̥ɔ/ f. thamba ‘woman’ /ˈt̪amba/ ... In Rimanggudinhma, the remaining initial vowels can be lost or retained, leading to VˈCV, ˈCV, VˈCVCV and ˈCVCV. Word minimality requirements also seem to play a role, in that monosyllables can be ‘repaired’ though the addition of an empty prefix consisting of a low vowel and a liquid, which adds aLˈCV to the inventory. ... (23) Rimanggudinhma a. VˈCV ako ‘bone’ /aˈkɔ/ b. ˈCV dharr ‘saltwater crocodile’ /ˈd̪ar/ c. VˈCVCV ilatyarr ‘black ibis’ /iˈlacar/ d. ˈCVCV mbana ‘own’ /ˈmbana/ e. aLˈCV alnggol ‘hole’ /alˈŋɡɔl/ ... This survey demonstrates how developments in root shape can easily turn a fairly complex Umpithamu-style system into a simple onset-sensitive one, characterised by stress on the first consonant-initial syllable. [Laycock 1969: 78] Stress is probably phonemic, if the evidence of P íbal 'quickly'/ipáy 'south' is trustworthy. Nevertheless, by far the most common stress placement is on the first syllable beginning with a consonant; accordingly, stress is marked only when this is not the case.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first syllable that begins with a consonant: the initial syllable in consonant-initial words, and the second syllable in vowel-initial words (which are common because of historical initial-consonant/syllable loss). Laycock thinks stress is probably phonemic on the strength of one Rimanggudinhma (P) minimal pair, íbal 'quickly' vs ipáy 'south', and marks stress in his transcriptions only where it departs from the default.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. p. 77 adds that all unstressed vowels in Lamalamic languages tend towards [ə], and that in U (Umbuygamu) phonetically geminate consonants may be a conditioned effect of 'the very heavy stress on the following syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'probably phonemic': P íbal 'quickly' vs ipáy 'south' (the only cited contrast); stress is marked in the wordlist only when it is not on the first consonant-initial syllable. The author cautions (p. 75) that 'a definitive phonology of Lamalamic languages is not possible here' because of poor 1964 recordings.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement on isolated citation forms from elicited vocabulary and short sentences (2 h of tape from one P speaker). The sentence is stated for the three Lamalamic languages jointly (L Lamalama, P Rimanggudinhma, U Umbuygamu), not separately for Rimanggudinhma; the phonemic-stress evidence is from P.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened statement is Laycock 1969, who pools the three Lamalamic languages: L = Lamalama [lby], P = "Parimankutinma/Parimangutinma" (= Rimanggudinhma, mbar1253; Laycock's spelling is listed as an alternate name on Wikipedia/AUSTLANG Y195), U = Umbuykamu (= Umbuygamu/Morrobalama, umbu1256). The stress sentence is stated for "Lamalamic languages" jointly, with the minimal pair for phonemic stress drawn from P (Rimanggudinhma). P data = one speaker, Winnie Kalakala, 2 h of tape recorded at Coen, Nov. 1964 (p. 75). Verstraete 2018 (OL 57:1, p. 4) says the archival corpus for Rimanggudinhma represents five speakers and that its phonological analysis differs significantly from the earlier sketches (Godman 1993), so a modern statement may supersede Laycock.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Laycock 1969 p. 78 statement ('by far the most common stress placement is on the first syllable beginning with a consonant'): first consonant-initial syllable. Adds an explicit onset-sensitive analysis, root-shape inventory, and the trisyllable exception; does not repeat Laycock's 'probably phonemic' hedge.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Onset-sensitive fixed stress: primary stress falls on the first consonant-initial syllable of the root, so vowel-initial roots (ako, ilatyarr, alnggol) stress the second syllable and consonant-initial roots (dharr, mbana, thamba) the first; described jointly for the three Lamalamic languages with Rimanggudinhma examples from Verstraete's 2017 dictionary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated for Rimanggudinhma (secondary stress is discussed only for Umpithamu).
new_statements.exceptions: pp. 28-29: consonant-initial trisyllabic roots (a small minority in all Lamalamic languages, probably old compounds) vary between first- and second-syllable stress, 'and the precise distribution and explanation of this stress variation remains unclear' (examples given for Lamalama, not Rimanggudinhma). Monosyllables may be repaired with an aL- prefix, giving aLˈCV.
new_statements.identity_note: Laycock 1969 labels the language 'P' = Parimankutinma, the name given by his sole informant Winnie Kalakala (recorded Coen, Nov. 1964); Glottolog lists Parimankutinma as an alternate name of mbar1253, and Verstraete 2018 (OL 57:1) confirms Laycock's P is Rimanggudinhma. Verstraete 2021's Rimanggudinhma data come from archival recordings of five speakers and his 2017 dictionary app; his stress generalisation is stated for the three Lamalamic languages jointly (Umbuygamu, Lamalama, Rimanggudinhma), with Rimanggudinhma-specific examples. Godman 1993 (unread) describes the same language from the Princess Charlotte Bay data.
